title: Undoing local changes: restore and reset
explanation:
Pick the undo command by *which layer* you want to change: the working directory, the index, or the branch pointer.

- `git restore <file>` replaces the file in your working directory with the last staged or committed version. **Any local changes to that file are gone** — only use it when you are sure.
- `git restore --staged <file>` unstages: the index goes back to HEAD's version, your working file is untouched.
- `git reset <commit>` moves the **current branch pointer** to `<commit>` and then, depending on the mode, keeps going:

| Mode | Moves branch | Resets index | Resets working directory |
|---|---|---|---|
| `--soft` | yes | no | no |
| `--mixed` (default) | yes | yes | no |
| `--hard` | yes | yes | **yes** |

So `git reset --soft HEAD~1` undoes the last commit but leaves its changes staged, `--mixed` also unstages them, and `--hard` throws them away. `--hard` is the one form of reset that destroys data: uncommitted work it overwrites cannot be recovered. Committed work usually can (see the next lesson).
keyIdeas: `git restore <file>` discards working-directory edits to that file (permanently).
`reset --soft` moves the branch; `--mixed` also resets the index; `--hard` also resets files.
`--hard` and `restore <file>` destroy uncommitted work — double-check first.

workedExample.problem: Starting from three commits A → B → C on `trunk`, show what each reset mode does when you move the branch back to commit A, returning to C in between.
steps: Remember A's id: `a=$(git rev-parse HEAD~2)`. Any commit reference works as the target of a reset.
`git reset --soft "$a"`: the branch points at A, and the changes from B and C are all staged (`git diff --name-only --cached` lists `log.md`).
Return to C with `git reset --hard ORIG_HEAD` (reset saves the previous tip in `ORIG_HEAD`).
`git reset --mixed "$a"`: branch at A, index matches A, but the file on disk still contains B and C's lines (unstaged). Then `git reset --hard "$a"`: branch, index, and file all match A.

Run it in a throwaway folder:
```sh
git init -q -b trunk shop && cd shop
for step in A B C; do echo "$step" >> log.md; git add log.md; git commit -q -m "$step"; done
a=$(git rev-parse HEAD~2)
git reset -q --soft "$a"
[ "$(git log -1 --format=%s)" = A ]
[ -n "$(git diff --name-only --cached)" ]   # B and C are staged
[ -z "$(git diff --name-only)" ]            # nothing unstaged
git reset -q --hard ORIG_HEAD
[ "$(git log -1 --format=%s)" = C ]
git reset -q --mixed "$a"
[ -z "$(git diff --name-only --cached)" ]   # index matches A
[ -n "$(git diff --name-only)" ]            # B and C are unstaged edits
grep -q C log.md
git reset -q --hard ORIG_HEAD
git reset -q --hard "$a"
[ -z "$(git diff --name-only)" ]
[ "$(cat log.md)" = A ]                   # B and C are gone from disk
echo ok
```
workedExample.answer: `--soft`: branch at A, B+C staged. `--mixed`: branch at A, B+C unstaged in the files. `--hard`: everything at A, the B+C edits are gone from disk (here recoverable only because they were committed).

pitfalls: Using `git reset --hard` to unstage a file — it also wipes your edits; use `git restore --staged`.
Running `git restore <file>` on work you hadn't committed and losing it for good.
Resetting commits that are already pushed; for shared history create a reverting commit instead.

citations.quote: It's important to understand that git restore <file> is a dangerous command. Any local changes you made to that file are gone — Git just replaced that file with the last staged or committed version.
citations.locator: Unmodifying a Modified File with git restore

citations.quote: Right below the "Changes to be committed" text, it says use git restore --staged <file>... to unstage.
citations.locator: Unstaging a Staged File with git restore

citations.quote: The reset command overwrites these three trees in a specific order, stopping when you tell it to: Move the branch HEAD points to (stop here if --soft).
Make the index look like HEAD (stop here unless --hard). Make the working directory look like the index.
If you specify the --mixed option, reset will stop at this point. This is also the default
It's important to note that this flag (--hard) is the only way to make the reset command dangerous, and one of the very few cases where Git will actually destroy data.
